itens.titulo: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang steps down after scandal, succeeded by CFO Colette Kress
itens.texto: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with a possible asset for China’s intelligence agency threw the GPU giant into turmoil, leading to Huang’s apologetic resignation and the Nvidia board’s appointments of Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones as its first chairman. The scandal brought renewed attention to Nvidia’s central role as a funder of and supplier to the global AI ecosystem, along with China-based companies’ access to advanced AI chips. What’s new: Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with Huang Le, who is also known as Alice Huang (the two are unrelated) as early as 2023. Ms. Huang held a high position at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that supplies processing power to Chinese AI companies. Unusually, U.S. intelligence personnel concluded in 2025 that Ms. Huang was passing information to China, but did not provide a defensive briefing to Mr. Huang or Nvidia, which is typical practice when U.S. citizens or companies are known targets of a foreign intelligence service. After allegations that Ms. Huang was a spy were published in The New York Times , Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation into the matter. A relationship with an employee also came to light, and Mr. Huang resigned. There are no indications that Jensen Huang knew that Ms. Huang was a spy. How it works: Nvidia designs the most capable chips for training and running AI. The U.S. government restricts exports of Nvidia’s most capable products to China, but the policy has proven porous: the company’s latest chips can legally reach Southeast Asia, where data centers like Megaspeed’s serve China-based customers. Jensen Huang has opposed export restrictions throughout, arguing that their main effect is to push China to build its own chip industry. Eventually, Nvidia and the Trump administration reached a compromise: Nvidia could sell some of its H200 chips directly to China, while the U.S. would charge a 25 percent export tariff. Exports of Nvidia’s most powerful B200 and B300 GPUs would still be barred to China. But China moved to block U.S. chip imports, claiming that Nvidia GPUs could enable U.S. spying. Instead, China has pressed its own chip designers and fabricators to build domestic substitutes. Between June 2024 and February 2026, a Megaspeed affiliate in Malaysia spent $4.8 billion on Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure, The New York Times reported . In late 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department investigated a Megaspeed site in Malaysia and found Nvidia chips still in their boxes, as though staged for shipment elsewhere. Nvidia later said it had reviewed the situation and found no evidence to support suspicions that Megaspeed was evading U.S. restrictions. Speculations about Ms. Huang's role were published in 2025. Megaspeed claimed that Ms. Huang left the company in August of that year. She is believed to have left Singapore and returned to Beijing at that time. In mid-2025, the U.S. government probed Megaspeed on suspicion that it had diverted chips to China, claims both Nvidia and Megaspeed denied. At this time, Nvidia said it stopped selling Megaspeed chips. Nvidia also stopped separately reporting GPU sales to Singapore. Also in 2025, U.S. government officials learned of Jensen Huang’s relationship with Huang Le. In spring 2026, a top-secret memo circulated among senior officials, including President Trump, asserting that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Ms. Huang to gather information about Jensen Huang that might help Beijing evade U.S. export restrictions. Reporters at The New York Times made Jensen Huang’s relationship  with Huang Le public in late October 2026, along with the charge that Ms. Huang gathered information for Chinese intelligence. On November 11, Nvidia’s board convened an emergency meeting, then announced a CEO transition . Jensen Huang resigned and Colette Kress assumed duties as interim CEO. Less than a week later, Mr. Huang announced that he would resume CEO duties if asked. But newly appointed chair Harvey Jones said on an earnings call for investors that the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not have plans to reinstate him. Yes, but: Jensen Huang’s position on selling GPUs to China was established long before his relationship with Ms. Huang. As Nvidia's CEO, his responsibility was to grow the business, including in the world’s largest market. As an American and Taiwanese citizen, he consistently argued that selling chips to mainland China was good for U.S. and Taiwanese security, since it would make China more dependent on U.S. and Taiwanese technology. Further, he shared this view with many other government and business leaders. Why it matters: Mr. Huang’s tenure tremendously benefitted the field of AI by providing critical computing technology to developers large and small. The rapid rise of AI put his company at the heart of U.S. national economics and security. Nvidia became the leading supplier of AI chips, responsible for 90 percent of all semiconductor revenue, and, for a time, the most valuable public company in the world. Nvidia under Huang was among the biggest boosters of open weight AI models, whether through its own Nemotron series, its acquisition of Hugging Face, or support for models outside its own ecosystem. Moreover, Nvidia privately funds Anthropic, OpenAI, and Safe SuperIntelligence; invests in CoreWeave, Nebius, Nokia, and xAI; and provides financial support and equipment for the world’s largest data center projects. Under interim CEO Kress (and a great deal more scrutiny from investors and regulators), Nvidia has promised to be more “disciplined” in its capital investments, signaling that its role as an AI “lender of last resort” might be gradually curtailed. itens.titulo: Jensen Huang's Legacy and Future: How Nvidia's founder saw opportunities other people couldn't
itens.texto: Dear friends, I was saddened to hear about Jensen Huang resigning from Nvidia last week. Yes, Jensen made serious mistakes . At the same time, he is a brilliant leader that has done tremendous work growing AI — providing compute to power training and inference, championing open source, and more — while turning Nvidia into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Much has been written about Jensen’s unique contributions. I still remember years ago, when I made my early push to use GPUs for training neural networks . Jensen met this idea with a positive reception, and he provided resources to help my teams at Stanford and Google and — long before it was obvious to most people that this was a good idea — directed Nvidia to shift to serving deep learning workloads. This bold call was one of many that led to Nvidia’s success. I appreciate particularly that, to ensure Nvidia’s success, he focused on building a thriving AI ecosystem that enabled many other teams to flourish. In many large companies, there is a mantra that no one is irreplaceable. In hindsight, this statement certainly did not apply to Jensen. Nvidia’s board may yet reinstate him as CEO, but if not, I wonder what future contributions he could have made to Nvidia that we will miss out on — and never know we missed. I hope everyone will see in Jensen’s critical role a refutation of the idea that people are replaceable. We should try to build teams that are robust enough to survive any individual’s departure. But at the same time, we should try to make contributions that others will look back on and understand were indispensable. Jensen is a hero of the AI world. When I wrote the blurb for his TIME 100 Award , I remember thinking there was so much more I could have written about him than would fit in the word count. I’m confident he will continue to make huge contributions. Let us all take inspiration from his example of the difference a single person can make and strive to contribute as much as we can. Keep building! Andrew

itens.titulo: GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol cut prices to match Claude: Alibaba updates to Qwen4; developers await open models
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: All the new models announced at Microsoft Ignite MDASH, a GitHub scanner that fixes bugs, not just reports them Nvidia’s board chair says no to reinstating Jensen Huang Nvidia halts sales of last-generation H200 GPUs to China But first: GPT-6.2 Astra leads all models in scientific work Artificial Analysis reports that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra places second on its Intelligence Index, behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2. Astra gained 5 points over GPT-6 Astra and now sits above Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and Claude Opus 5.5 (59) at top effort settings, while GPT-6.2 Sol gained 2 points to reach 57, matching GPT-6 Astra at about 15 percent of the cost per task. Astra is priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, 20 percent below GPT-6 Astra, with cached input cut to $0.40 from $1.00; Sol stays at $2 and $10. The models lead the site’s science, 3D and robotics evaluations, but the Coding Agent Index is flat for Astra and down 3 points for Sol, and both hallucinate often on factual questions (59 percent for Astra, 55 percent for Sol at max effort). For most software developers, the results suggest that coding-heavy workloads gain little from the upgrade, while the Sol result and the lower Astra price give cheaper options for science, knowledge and agentic work. ( Artificial Analysis ) Alibaba debuts new flagship proprietary model Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, its newest large language model, on Alibaba’s cloud platform. The model has 2.4 trillion parameters but activates only 71 billion at a time, backed by 328 billion N-gram parameters that cache frequently repeated calculations. Its training uses a residual connection (a shortcut that lets gradients skip layers) with four gated channels instead of the usual single one, and its attention mechanism adds Gated DeltaNet and QSA to cut hardware needs and skip unneeded data. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding challenges, Alibaba says Qwen4-Max beat Qwen3.8-Max while using up to 49% fewer tokens. Alibaba also open-sourced Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, which has the model return a quick first draft and refine it as users give feedback, and plans to open-source smaller models built on the same techniques later. This model is proprietary, but Alibaba said it would release smaller open weight models in the Qwen4 family. ( Silicon Angle ) Microsoft debuts models for coding, images, updated Copilot Microsoft announced six AI models at its Ignite conference, covering coding, cybersecurity, image generation, transcription and real-time voice. The lead model, MAI Code 2, delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s performance at 40% of the price and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s at 5% of the cost, according to Microsoft. MAI Code 2 Flash is a smaller model that Microsoft says matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and MAI Cyber 2 Flash is said to beat GPT-6 Astra on a security benchmark at under 2% of the cost per task. The comparisons use selected benchmarks, some of the price gaps reflect promotional discounts, and Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman acknowledged a model tuned for everyday coding will be weaker at advanced math or science. MAI Code 2 will be available in GitHub Copilot, and enterprise customers can license model weights to customize with their own data, but only on Azure, so Copilot users may soon be running Microsoft’s own models in place of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. ( Axios ) GitHub study focuses on AI bug fixes, not just reports GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot in which Microsoft’s Codename MDASH scanner, which uses the MAI Cyber model, looked for security bugs in six open source projects: AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty. It flagged thousands of possible issues. A GitHub Security Lab triage agent removed duplicates and invalid findings, then seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers spent about two days per project verifying the rest by hand. That left 99 reports, sent privately through GitHub’s private vulnerability reporting, each with a suggested fix. As of November 15, maintainers had fixed 55 of them, 14 in a release; Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of theirs within a week, and an ImageMagick maintainer said a report that normally takes 30 to 60 minutes to read and fix took 15. The authors note that six projects is a small sample and that the manual review does not scale yet. The pilot’s model for AI-assisted reporting is to check each finding against the project’s threat model and security policy, report it privately, and include a fix — the researchers note that AI-assisted bug reports are plentiful, but AI bug fixes remain scarce. ( GitHub ) Nvidia board not interested in bringing back Jensen Huang On Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call, new board chair Harvey Jones said the board unanimously accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. Jones said the board would not take questions on the circumstances of the resignation or the ongoing investigation. Earlier the same day, Huang posted on X that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone,” and would cooperate with the board’s investigation, but offered to return as CEO if the board decided that was best for the company. Since his November 12th resignation, stories about Huang have focused on multiple reported marital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st. For developers who depend on Nvidia hardware and CUDA, the call offered no long-term successor or product guidance, so the company’s near-term direction depends on the internal investigation and the congressional testimony. itens.titulo: Gemini 4 Hydrogen balances accuracy and speed: Open source llama.cpp finally reaches version 1.0.0
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Jensen Huang steps down, Colette Kress named interim CEO Google releases most promising decision model yet Runway’s Praxis-1 leads on robotics simulation benchmark Cloud-native developers top 21 million, strain open source But first: Google debuts a fast model to complement Carbon, replace 3.8 Flash Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster model in the Gemini 4 family than Carbon and Argon, and made it available across AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini app, Search, and Google Antigravity. Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across a 1 million-token context window, with four thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default), and a new xhigh. Google says Hydrogen scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at the default level (54 at xhigh) against Argon’s 50, and finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google also added Orchestrator to Antigravity, which switches between models such as Carbon and Hydrogen within one session; on Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reached near-Carbon success rates while using 24% less quota and finishing 19% faster, by Google’s measurement. Teams on Gemini 3.8 Flash have a cheaper, faster migration target, and Orchestrator offers a way to split planning and execution across models without managing the routing themselves. ( Google ) Llama.cpp gets first major update since 2023 The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face released v1.0.0 of both libllama and libggml, the project’s first major version after about 3.5 years of development. From now on, breaking changes to the public C API or ABI in each library’s include directory will trigger a major-version bump, while backward-compatible features, backend updates, and model support get minor bumps and bug fixes get patches. The project now ships through Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget, and an XCFramework for iOS and macOS, plus pre-release artifacts for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS. It supports more than 150 model architecture variants and the mainstream speculative decoding methods, and runs CI on self-hosted runners with hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM, and Intel. Developers who link against libllama or libggml can now treat the version number as a signal for when an upgrade will break their build, and can pin to a major version in package managers. ( Hugging Face ) Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigns Following his admission of an extramarital affair and a rapid third-party investigation, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately, after 33 years at the company. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and the board has begun a search that will consider internal and external candidates. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys CEO, was appointed the board’s first-ever chair. The company says operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap will continue without interruption, and the third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings report stays scheduled for November 17. ( Nvidia ) Google releases decision model that rivals Jev at higher price Google released the Gemini Decisions API, backed by a new model, gemini-decision-1, that returns calibrated probabilities for typed questions instead of generating text. One request takes a shared input (text, image, audio, video, or PDF) and up to 1,000 questions, each a yes/no, a choice among 2 to 255 options, or a score on a rubric of up to 255 levels. Input costs $0.10 per 1M tokens, output tokens are always zero, and the shared input is billed once per request; Google reports 150-250 ms end-to-end latency for inputs up to 16K tokens. In Google’s self-reported benchmarks, the model leads 7 of 9 accuracy tests and has a top-1 calibration error of 0.0250, about half the 0.0494 of TypeSafe Jev1.14, but it trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%) and Mind2Web Multimodal (86.2% vs 86.8%) and costs more per token ($0.10 vs $0.042). It runs only on Google’s hosted API, with a 262,144-token context and no prompt caching or Batch API. For agent builders, this replaces generate-then-parse for routing, policy checks and grading with numeric outputs they can branch on. Note that the benchmark figures are unverified and repeated context is billed in full on every call. ( MarkTechPost ) Runway publishes open-weight robotics model Runway released Praxis-1, a robot control model, with open weights and source code under the commercial-use-friendly Apache 2.0 license. The model takes camera images, text instructions, and the robot’s position data, predicts how the scene will change, and outputs matching robot movements. It builds on a video model fine-tuned with human-action videos and robot data, and it still needs adaptation per robot: about 277 hours of DROID data for a Franka arm, and 1,400 to 2,600 hours for a dual-arm robot. On Nvidia’s RoboLab-120 simulation leaderboard Runway reports a 46.2 percent success rate, ahead of FLUX 3 Action at 42.9 percent among World Action Models. Note that Runway ran the tests itself and they are not independently verified. For developers, the weights and code are on Hugging Face and GitHub. However, the standard model needs an 80 GB GPU; the compressed version is estimated to fit a 32 GB RTX 5090 without a measured memory figure. ( The Decoder ) Cloud-native developers grow by millions, lead AI adoption The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and research firm SlashData’s latest State of Cloud Native Development report counts more than 21 million cloud-native developers, or 41% of developers worldwide. About 75% of them use AI in some form, compared with about 55% of other developers, according to SlashData’s Liam Bollmann-Dodd. CNCF’s Bob Killen said the headcount likely undercounts, since many people consume cloud-native applications without knowing it.

itens.titulo: Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs: An agent that searches, outlines, and reads entire documents outperforms chunk-and-embed retrieval
itens.texto: Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks. How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro. The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges. Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s). Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read. Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent) Why it matters: Chunk-and-embed retrieval methods tend not to work well with documents in which the meaning of any given passage is not self-contained, such as financial reports, contracts, and regulatory filings. In such cases, letting a model search the whole document is more effective. We’re thinking: Chunk-and-embed has its place, but letting agents write search queries can be a better approach. Beyond READ and RLM (covered in last week’s issue of The Batch ), Search-R1 trains LLMs to reason their way through multi-turn searches, and IRCoT uses an LLM’s reasoning traces as a search query.

itens.titulo: Search Engine Wars, AI Edition: Google makes less money on LLM-powered search even as OpenAI works to attract its users
itens.texto: Google is turning its search engine into a chatbot, and OpenAI is turning its chatbot into a search engine. Yet neither company has made AI-powered search bring in as much revenue per query as traditional search links. What’s new: On October 29, the day after Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported its financial statement for July through September, its market value fell by nearly $500 billion, its biggest one-day decline on record, The Wall Street Journal reported . Google’s search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent, down from 19 percent and 17 percent in the previous two quarters. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s business expanded, presumably including many queries that once would have been entered into a search engine. An OpenAI executive said ChatGPT’s weekly users had grown from 1 billion to 1.2 billion in two months, and it claims to handle roughly one-fifth as many searches as Google. How Google search pays: Google makes money when advertisers pay for their messages to appear beside search results, but that business is shrinking. Google collected $63.35 billion from traditional search and related ads from July through September, including ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode. The number of queries it received grew at its fastest rate in five years Google didn’t reveal how much of that revenue came from AI Mode, but an AI Mode query brings in less revenue than a comparable traditional search, because it shows fewer ads and advertisers pay less for them, Ars Technica wrote . In effect, Google’s AI is cannibalizing its search business. How AI search ads work: Meanwhile, both Google and OpenAI are pushing ads into AI-generated search results. On the day it issued its financial report, Google said AI Mode will show ads in 11 countries , up from 1 previously. In the U.S., ads will appear when a user enters a follow-up query. OpenAI, which began to test ads early this year, now shows them in 89 countries to users of ChatGPT's free and low-cost Go plans. OpenAI says its ad sales reached a pace of $1 billion per year within 200 days of launch, a figure that hasn't been verified independently. That works out to about $250 million every three months, compared with Google's $63.35 billion. Yes, but: OpenAI is a private company, so it's impossible to assess how much of Google's search business ChatGPT actually has taken, and estimates vary widely. When it said it processed one-fifth the number of searches Google does, it didn’t explain which Google figure it compared against, Search Engine Journal noted . In February, the search-marketing firm Ahrefs estimated 12 percent, using a different definition of search. Behind the news: While Google and OpenAI compete for AI-powered search, the web publishers whose pages AI models use to generate search results are seeking more control over how AI companies use their work. One proposal would let them put a flag on their pages that would ask AI developers not to use them to train models. Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic said they plan to honor the flag. Meanwhile, Google offers publishers a way to exempt their pages from AI Overviews and AI Mode. Why it matters: AI has many uses, but it’s not yet entirely clear how to build highly profitable businesses on it. AI-powered search could be one answer, since advertisers already pay to reach users through search engines. Ironically, AI is drawing more people to search faster than it’s drawing advertising money. But until AI search ads earn as much as the traditional ads they replace, relying purely on AI search for revenue doesn’t seem like a surefire way to replicate Google’s previous success. We’re thinking: Chatbots may eventually eat into users’ web searches, but the users of the future won’t necessarily be people. AI agents carrying out tasks such as shopping on a user's behalf will also see ads that could sway their behavior or recommendations to users. In fact, Time magazine already sells ads aimed at agents instead of people .

itens.titulo: LLMs Can Fine-Tune Neural Networks: Researchers used GPT-6 Astra to improve a small model’s performance by editing its weights
itens.texto: Research suggests that you can improve a neural network’s weights simply by prompting an LLM — for networks of less than 1 billion parameters, at least. What’s new: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, and colleagues from MIT showed that GPT-6 Astra can interpret, improve, and produce neural network weights in proof-of-concept studies . How it works: The authors asked GPT-6 Astra to (a) identify which game a network was trained on based on its weights, (b) alter the weights of a network to improve its ability to operate a simulated car, and (c) generate a network that would win a game. In a more practical experiment, they asked GPT-6 Astra to improve Qwen3.5-0.8B’s math performance. The authors trained four tiny vanilla neural networks (17,000 parameters each) separately to play Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Frogger. Given the weights and asked “Which game was this neural network trained on?” GPT-6 Astra was able to identify the game in all four cases. The authors trained a vanilla neural network (171,000 parameters) to drive a car up a ramp in the Kinetix environment but suspended the training when the car failed to climb the ramp. They fed GPT-6 Astra a description of the problem, the goal, the model weights, and one of the actions the model took during a failed run. GPT-6 Astra edited 3.5 percent of the vanilla neural network’s weights, enabling it to succeed in all 1,024 attempts. They gave GPT-6 Astra the rules and source code of a game (specifically Breakout, Seaquest, or Asterix) and a 20,000-parameter network whose weights were initialized to 0, and asked it to generate a model that would play the game. They trained networks of the same size and type for comparison. The generated models achieved higher scores than the manually trained ones at 100 million training steps. However, the trained models were more competitive at 500 million training steps: Of the three games, Astra led on one, roughly tied on one, and lost on the third. GPT-6 Astra, given Qwen3.5-0.8B’s weights, a tool to run it, and the training set for the MATH-500 and GSM8K math benchmarks, was asked to improve its benchmark performance. It found that Qwen3.5-0.8B often looped, filling its context window unnecessarily, and modified 0.016 percent of the weights. The change boosted performance on MATH-500 from 7.9 percent to 48.1 percent. Yes, but: Not all case studies yielded positive results. Asking GPT-6 Astra to improve Gemma 3 270M’s math performance did not work. GPT-6 Astra didn’t find any looping or other obvious issue, and so it was unable to improve the Gemma 3 270M’s performance. Why it matters: These results are proofs of concept that have not been shown to extend to more diverse LLMs and target models. However, they show how LLMs could be used in building models. They might improve interpretability, enabling us to better understand the networks we build. Or they might facilitate network editing or generation, making it possible to diagnose and fix obvious issues or accelerate training. We're thinking: If neural network editing holds true at larger scales, this holds massive promise: It’s much cheaper to run a network once than to fine-tune one.

itens.titulo: GPT-6 Cyber Patches More Security Flaws for Less Cost: OpenAI’s security-tuned version of GPT-6 Astra closed root-level Linux holes for $1,280 each
itens.texto: OpenAI built a cybersecurity model that discovered, exploited, and patched nearly 950 severe vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel in a single run. What’s new: GPT-6 Cyber , a version of GPT-6 Astra fine-tuned to find software vulnerabilities, is restricted initially to approved customers. In a mid-October scan of the Linux kernel, GPT-6 Cyber generated working exploits for 948 flaws that allow ordinary users to gain full control of a machine. The run cost $1,213,430 in API calls, around $1,279 per exploit. (In July, the same harness running GPT-5.6 Sol exploited 166 such vulnerabilities for a total cost of $513,690, around $3,095 per exploit.) Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1,050,000 tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens) Features: Reasoning, tool use, streaming, structured outputs Performance: More capable than GPT-6 Astra on most tests of cybersecurity conducted by OpenAI Availability: Initially offered to selected customers of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red advanced security program; customers must use single sign-on, multifactor authentication, managed devices, and least-privileged access and restrict API requests to specific IP addresses Price: API $20/$2/$100 per million input/cached/output tokens; cache storage $25 per million tokens for 30 minutes, $50 per million tokens for 12 hours License: Proprietary Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data, training details, knowledge cutoff, reasoning levels, schedule for wider availability How it works: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-6 Cyber via reinforcement learning on tasks such as reproducing crashes, generating working exploits, and finding code vulnerabilities. The reward function discouraged refusal of authorized security requests and reward hacking, and it encouraged the model to stay within authorized behaviors and to report results accurately. A team of agents ran a pipeline that enabled the model to find, confirm, and exploit flaws in the Linux kernel and patch them. In the pipeline, scout agents identified security-relevant parts of the kernel that ordinary users can reach. Analyst agents read the scout agents’ candidate code and flagged 2,308 flaws within 12 hours. For each candidate, a triage agent wrote a short program to trigger the flaw in a virtual machine that detected memory errors. The triage agent iterated until the flaw appeared or the agent ran out of approaches. This step confirmed 1,724 flaws within 30 hours. A screening agent reviewed the confirmed flaws and kept those that had a plausible path to root access that would confer full control of a machine. Exploit-writing agents tried to gain root access in virtual machines configured with a standard Linux distribution’s protections and produced 1,169 working exploits. The pipeline wrote patches and checked nearby code for variants of each flaw. Security researchers reviewed the exploits and proposed severity ratings before reporting them to Linux maintainers. Performance: GPT-6 Cyber proved substantially more capable than GPT-5.6 Cyber in tests by OpenAI, and it outperformed GPT-6 Astra on most benchmarks. Independent tests have not yet been published. On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT-6 Cyber set to the highest reasoning level tested (48.45 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra set to its highest level (42.43 percent) and GPT-5.6 Cyber (32.1 percent). On a version of ExploitGym with stronger defenses, GPT-6 Cyber (36.94 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra (29.69 percent). Gemini 4 Carbon, evaluated by Google without guardrails at an undisclosed reasoning level, achieved 54.8 percent. ExploitGym Honeypot instructs a model to exploit a specific target but includes an easy-to-exploit supporting service that the model may use but isn’t authorized to attack. GPT-6 Cyber attacked that service in 0.07 percent of attempts without OpenAI’s safety deployment instructions, compared with 5.51 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber and 0 percent for GPT-6 Astra. With the instructions, GPT-6 Cyber did not attack the honeypot. On FrontierCyber, 288 real-world challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved 90 and GPT-6 Astra solved 96. Neither model solved any of the 15 hardest challenges, nor did they successfully attack a fully hardened target. Behind the news: The cybersecurity capabilities of recent top-performing AI models — which are available either in guardrailed versions or to selected customers — have set security personnel on high alert. In October, the U.S. government reported critical flaws in the PHP server coding language after OpenAI had led a coalition that addressed them in preceding months. Hackers stole $6.3 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the biggest known crypto heist, by exploiting compromised internal AI tools. Why it matters: The latest cybersecurity models pose both challenges and opportunities for security. On one hand, they’re extremely adept at exploiting flaws. On the other, they make flaws easy and inexpensive to find and fix. Hacking competitions like Pwn2Own have offered $20,000 to $70,000 per Linux kernel exploit, yet OpenAI spent $1,279 per exploit. We’re thinking: It’s encouraging that GPT-6 Cyber without safety instructions exploited the off-limits service in only 0.07 percent of attempts in OpenAI’s honeypot test, and with safety instructions never tried. We’d like to see OpenAI help independent testers to repeat this test or others like it.

itens.titulo: How to Build an Agent Harness in One Prompt: Build agent harnesses for any LLM using the open source OpenWorker Agent Harness SDK
itens.texto: Dear friends, Building an agent harness has been a rapidly growing method to build an AI agent. The OpenWorker project just released the open source OpenWorker Agent Harness SDK , which I invite you to check out. If you have not built an agent harness before, I encourage you to do so. (This skill is reflected in the AI Engineering Skills Map , and job interviews increasingly ask people if they’ve done this.) This letter describes how to steer coding agents to quickly build an agent harness. An agent harness is the code that wraps around an LLM and provides it with context, tools, and guardrails to turn it into an application. Since late last year, LLMs have become powerful enough that it’s practical to build many applications by repeatedly calling an LLM and letting it decide what to do next. For example, you might build your own coding agent by giving it tools (functions) to read/save files, run shell commands, execute code the agent has written, and read output of the executed code. Given these tools, you can build a simple coding agent that can save code to a file, run it, see if there are any errors, and iterate to improve the code. To take a second example, here’s how you can build a simple demo agent that organizes files. First, in a new/empty project directory, run in bash: npx @openworkerai/openworker-harness-builder --agent claude --project. Replace “claude” above with “codex” if your coding agent is Codex. This should install OpenWorker’s openworker-harness-builder in the current directory. Then, prompt your coding agent with a prompt like: Use the openworker-harness-builder skill to build a small local file-organizing agent using the OpenWorker Harness SDK. Generate 10 sample text files in a dedicated demo directory. The app should have an agent that has tools to list and read files, create/delete subdirectories, and move files. Configure the harness such that all of these tools are restricted to only the demo directory. Use OPENAI_API_KEY in ~/.env and gpt-6.1-terra [or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and claude-sonnet-5-5]. Prompt the agent to organize files, create subdirectories, and move files into appropriate subdirectories to organize the files. Require user approval before each subdirectory creation and file move, showing the proposed operation. Display tool activity so the user can see what happens at each step of the demo. As it is running, also display a succinct description of the status of the agent loop so the user can see what’s happening. Building an agent harness requires managing LLM context. For long-running agents, this requires building a memory architecture (such as memory compaction when the context gets too long). A harness may also need guardrails (such as input/output checking), a mechanism for approvals, security controls (for example, keeping credentials away from the LLM), and sandboxing. OpenWorker Desktop is finding usage in many security workflows, and Rohit Prsad and I built the OpenWorker Harness SDK to make it easier to improve OpenWorker Desktop. But we were delighted to hear that several other groups found the Harness SDK useful for building other agents, which is why we’re releasing it as open source. You can use it to build agents that run locally or are deployed online. If you have not yet built an agent harness, please follow the steps above and give it a shot. Unlike the agent harness tools offered by model providers, OpenWorker’s Harness SDK is open source and not beholden to any model, so you can easily build agents that run with any model provider and on any cloud. Keep building! Andrew

itens.titulo: Anthropic releases new top models: Meta’s Muse Ember rivals leading fast models
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: AlphaProof Code verifies Signal’s cryptography algorithm Alibaba’s Co-Design Bench measures fully correct commits Google’s most powerful model now available for developers Anthropic ports Claude from Nvidia to AMD processors in three days But first: Claude updates Fable and Mythos ahead of IPO Anthropic released Fable 5.2 on Monday, with Mythos 5.2 going to select organizations through its existing verification program, days before a public listing expected as soon as this month. Fable 5.2 handles harder software engineering work, hardware tasks such as controlling robots, and long-running projects, and is designed to coordinate more than 1,000 AI agents at once. Mythos 5.2 is the same model with fewer safeguards for cybersecurity and life sciences work, and Anthropic is extending access to more US and non-US companies. Anthropic says both models are faster than earlier versions, and Fable now costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1. Anthropic says the US government and third-party evaluators reviewed the models before launch and that new sandbox-escape tests found both less likely to break out of testing environments than prior versions, though those test results were not published in the article. ( Anthropic ) Muse Ember matches Claude Haiku 5.5 at lower cost per task Artificial Analysis reports that Meta’s Muse Ember matches Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at 36 on its Intelligence Index while costing $0.14 per task versus $0.41. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 cached input, and $0.50 output. Input and output match Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna, but Artificial Analysis says cached input is 60% cheaper and Ember uses about a third as many output tokens. Agentic results are mixed: Ember beats Haiku on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (40.9% vs 32.8%) but trails on FrontierCode 2.0 (27.2% vs 34.9%). In Meta’s own Muse Code agent, the model scores 46 on the firm’s Coding Agent Index, against 37 for Haiku in Claude Code. Its AA-Omniscience accuracy is 21.1%, the lowest of comparable models, because it declines 64% of questions, which holds its hallucination rate to 17.4%, half of Haiku’s. For developers running high-volume agent workloads where cached input dominates the bill, Ember is a cheaper option on this benchmark data, though it is a weak fit for tasks that depend on factual recall. ( Artificial Analysis ) Google teams solve a major cryptography problem Google DeepMind researchers used an agentic AI framework called AlphaProof Code to formally verify several cryptographic guarantees of the Signal protocol, in a four-week proof-of-concept. Formal verification uses math to prove software behaves as specified. The work did not cover the entire Signal mobile app, and it found no new vulnerabilities in the portions examined. Run against older Signal versions with known, long-fixed flaws, the tool correctly flagged them and showed the protocol could not be verified. DeepMind is releasing its specification and proof for the Signal analysis, but Google declined to share the project’s cost or say whether a commercial product is planned, so whether AI-assisted verification can scale affordably to larger codebases is still open. ( Google ) AI code still requires human cleanup Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities released Co-Design Bench, a coding-agent benchmark built from real user change requests to existing web apps, some supplied as images, audio, video, or documents. In tests of ten models, the top performer, GPT-6 Astra, met about 70 percent of each task’s requirements on average but produced a fully correct result on only 26.4 percent of tasks. Scores fell for every model as a task combined more change types such as layout, design, interaction, and content, and extra compute did not help: GLM-5.2 used nearly six times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra on smaller changes and scored significantly worse. The same model also scored differently across harnesses (the programs through which an agent reads, writes, and executes code); Qwen3.8-27B got 75 percent in one environment and 56 percent in another on larger overhauls. For developers choosing a coding agent, this means a leaderboard score for the model alone is incomplete, and the model should be tested together with the harness it will run in. ( The Decoder ) Gemini 4 Carbon now widely available Google DeepMind made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business, after a two-week preview for security defenders in its Fairwind Program. Pricing matches Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and Google AI Ultra subscribers get it in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search. Google says Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than twice as low a cost per task as the next best external model, and second on a new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark built with Artificial Analysis. Carbon uses more tokens than Argon to reason and verify, so Google recommends Argon for most software engineering and knowledge work and Carbon for multi-step debugging and open-ended research. Google also previewed /swarm in Antigravity, which turns one prompt into a team of agents, with Carbon assigned to architecture, coordination, and auditing and lighter models handling parallel work. Because Carbon costs the same per token as Argon but spends more of them, developers will need to compare cost per task on their own workloads before routing hard problems to it. ( Google ) Anthropic engineers may have solved the CUDA problem Anthropic says it ported Claude to AMD GPUs in three days with almost no human intervention, a job that normally takes dozens of engineers six to twelve months. According to co-founder and Chief Compute Officer Tom Br

itens.titulo: All the fallout so far from Nvidia CEO’s affair: Inkling 2 Small jumps 18 points on Intelligence Index
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5 percent on ExploitGym Decision Index v2 weighs decision models’ accuracy, cost Pangram releases its first AI image, video detectors Nous reveals open Alibaba models’ shallow political alignment But first: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang under fire for affair with alleged spy Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang admitted on Nov. 8 to an affair, confirming reports that linked him to Alice Huang, a Megaspeed International executive. The New York Times reported on Nov. 6 that a Trump administration memo cited intelligence that a Chinese spy agency had recruited her to collect information about him; Beijing called a similar report “unsubstantiated and purely a smear.” Megaspeed is a Singapore-based compute-rental company that became one of the largest Asian buyers of Nvidia AI chips, with imports peaking above $4.6 billion, and the U.S. and Singapore are investigating its ownership and whether it smuggled chips to China. Nvidia says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” and House Republicans have requested a briefing from Huang. Whether the board’s findings affect Huang’s position is unresolved. Huang’s leadership shapes Nvidia’s supply allocation, its $500 billion AI financing effort, and its lobbying against chip export limits. ( Bloomberg ) Inkling’s latest would be best open model outside China Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, a proprietary reasoning model that scores 31 on the latest Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, up 18 points from Inkling Small and level with Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash. It has 594 billion total and 17 billion active parameters, takes text and image input, and is available only through Thinking Machines’ Tinker platform and Tinker Playground at $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens. Gains are largest on agentic work: AutomationBench-AA rose from 5% to 46% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 5% to 25%, though it scores 13% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 30% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium). It also uses about 150,000 output tokens per task, roughly four times Inkling Small, which raises its cost to $1.18 per task from $0.20, still below Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) at $7.77 and Sonnet 5.5 at $10.02. Thinking Machines plans an Apache 2.0 weights release but has no confirmed date. Artificial Analysis says that release would make this the top-scoring open weights model from outside China. ( Artificial Analysis ) OpenAI gives updated security model a limited release OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity-focused model that it says scores higher at exploiting vulnerabilities and goes out of bounds less than 1 percent of the time in testing, down from about 5 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber. On ExploitGym, a benchmark of vulnerability exploitation, it scored 48.5 percent, against 32.1 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber and 42.4 percent for OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra. The out-of-bounds figure comes from ExploitGym HoneyPot, an OpenAI evaluation modeled on the Hugging Face Incident, in which OpenAI’s agents breached Hugging Face while hunting for answers to a task. OpenAI classifies the model as Critical under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber, and says it helped find 81 previously unknown Firefox vulnerabilities. Access is limited to select members of the Daybreak Red program for authorized defensive security work, with all Daybreak Red customers to follow in the coming weeks, so most developers cannot use it yet. ( OpenAI ) Independent tests compare dedicated decision models, LLMs Artificial Analysis released Decision Index v2, a benchmark of decision models whose headline Decision Score rewards both correct answers and well-calibrated confidence. Private datasets now make up 45% of the Index, up from 25%, and it adds two new benchmarks: AA-Paperclip (30%), which scores 1,500 documents as correct only if all 15 answers are right, and AA-Symmetry (15%), which checks whether answers hold when equivalent questions are reworded. Drex Max v1.1 from Nace AI and GLiDE v1.2 from Fastino Labs lead the decision models at 73, with Mammoth 27B at 72, while the language models Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna score 77 and 76 at 15x the cost and about 40x the latency of Drex Max v1.1. Cost per 1M tasks ranges from $14 to $859 across decision models, and billing design matters as much as token price: GLiDE v1.2 bills a document’s input once per question, so it costs about eight times Drex Max v1.1 despite 33% higher list prices. The results show that a decision model that bills the document once and is well-calibrated can come within a few points of a frontier language model at a fraction of its cost and latency. ( Artificial Analysis ) Pangram unveils AI models to detect AI images, videos Pangram released Pangram Image 1.0 for AI image detection and Pangram Image Flash 1.0, a smaller, faster model that handles AI video detection. On Pangram’s own test of 1,200 synthetic images made by 12 generators from 100 real photos, Image 1.0 scored 99.96% accuracy. Image Flash scored 98.7% on the academic DF26 benchmark, which Pangram says is 29 points above the next best detector. Pangram also tested Image Flash 1.0 on 1,529 videos, pairing 129 real social media clips with AI versions from 14 generators. Image 1.0 now accepts images as small as 256x256, with a reduced-confidence notice below 512x512, and returns a heatmap showing where AI content appears. Both models are available through an updated API and a Chrome extension that flags AI content while browsing, and video uploads are analyzed frame by frame. Accuracy figures for image and video tests come from Pangram’s own evaluations, so developers considering the API may want to try it on their own samples before relying on them. itens.titulo: Context Engineering for Images: MIT researchers build VISTA, an agent harness that keeps images in memory for faster retrieval
itens.texto: Managing an agent’s context by storing all the input text it receives and giving it tools to search the text boosts its performance. For vision-language agents, the same is true of storing images. What’s new: Qiushi Han, Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, and colleagues at MIT released VISTA , an agent that completed the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark of interactive visual-reasoning puzzles using 57.4 percent fewer actions than humans who had not encountered them before. The VISTA harness is freely available under the MIT license. Key insight: Given an image frame from a videogame or other interactive environment, agentic systems typically embed it and keep the embedding until the context is full, at which point they delete it. This raises two issues: Embeddings are lossy and may not retain valuable information, and once an embedding has been deleted, the model no longer has access to information it contained. Storing all frames in a persistent memory retains all the information they carry, and enabling an agent to retrieve and zoom in on them makes it possible to embed details that otherwise may not have been captured. How it works: VISTA works with Anthropic Claude Opus 5.0 or OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol. Its harness works similarly to other popular harnesses, except it retains all input frames and includes a tool that retrieves frames. Given a new frame and list of available keyboard actions (such as left, right, up, down, spacebar, or click), the agent tells the model to decide whether to (i) read or update notes, (ii) retrieve previous frames, (iii) retrieve previous actions and their results, or (iv) execute an action. It repeats this choice until the model takes action. After the environment updates (during which it may produce a series of frames), it adds to the model’s input the last frame and a new list of available actions and executes the loop again. The agent maintains two notes: information it deduces about the environment that can be reused across levels or sessions (for example, the difference between a brown block and a black background), and information deduced about the level or problem at hand (for example, that the character currently has a power-up or conditions under which the model failed previously). The agent decides when to read these notes. When the agent decides to retrieve earlier frames, the tool enables it to retrieve any number of frames and zoom in to any part of a frame. During an attempt to complete a puzzle or game level, VISTA stores in memory not only images but also a list of actions and their results. It can decide to retrieve any set of previous actions or summaries of all previous attempts. Results: The authors tested VISTA on ARC-AGI-3 (25 games), GameWorld (170 tasks in 34 games), and AI GameStore (10 games). It enabled Claude Opus 5.0 and GPT-5.6 Sol to outperform earlier agents as well as humans who encountered the same challenges for the first time. On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA with Claude Opus 5.0 achieved a perfect score of 100 Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), meaning it completed all puzzles in fewer actions than first-time human players. (Earlier projects that achieved perfect RHAE scores, such as Tycho , generated programs that simulated the environments.) VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 99 RHAE. Denied the ability to store frames, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 70 RHAE, which shows that the frames were useful. On GameWorld, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 63.3 percent of tasks on average. First-time human players completed 55.3 percent, and the native harness with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 40 percent. On AI GameStore, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved a much higher score than first-time players and the native harness, 40 percent better than humans on average. Why it matters: Games and other interactive environments generate potentially endless streams of frames, each of which contain information an agent may not have deduced earlier. Only so many frames fit in its context, and not all frames are relevant at any given moment. By storing all frames and giving the agent tools to retrieve them, agents can find the relevant frames and re-examine them within the current context. We're thinking: Apparently context engineering helps whether the medium is text or images. Multimodal systems benefit from multimodal context management.

itens.titulo: World Models Become Robot Playgrounds: Google Genie 4 combines with Gemini models to build better video game worlds, robotics training
itens.texto: Google says that Genie 4, its latest world model, will be used in tandem with Gemini models to create digital practice spaces for robots, giving them endless worlds to train in. So far, though, Google’s demos suggest there’s still a long way to go. What’s new : On October 27, Google announced Genie 4 , which it has released to a limited group of testers in a research preview. Genie 4 produces interactive worlds that Google says are even more realistic than its predecessor, Genie 3. Users can change a scene midway through with a text prompt, but now Gemini models help work those changes into the scene. Genie 4 also adds sound, which allows it to create real-time audio for each world it generates, whether it’s two people chatting on a motorcycle or snow crunching under a crowned crane’s feet. Google AI Ultra subscribers as well as some developers should be getting access in the weeks ahead. How it works: Genie 4 doesn’t have a technical report out yet, but Google’s announcement explains how Gemini models can help direct what Genie 4 renders. Navigation : Users move through a scene with video game-style mouse and keyboard controls. Text directions: While Genie 4 renders a scene, Gemini 3.8 Flash works alongside it as a director. It breaks the user’s goal into steps, then double-checks each new frame to make sure each of those steps has been executed, adjusting its plan if the user inserts changes as things go along. Video: Gemini Omni , Google’s video generation model, helps Genie 4 render more realistic scenery. Google demoed examples including a maple seed gracefully spinning and landing on grass, as well as people shuffling along a 1980s-era train platform. Robotics: In a demo, Google’s reasoning model Gemini 4 Argon broke a task into text-based steps for Genie 4 while it rendered a simulation of Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers with a person. Google didn’t describe a robot control system in the loop. Results: Google’s announcement was full of curated demos, but the company didn’t offer any quantitative evaluations to back them up. Google says a simulation can run up to two minutes, roughly double Genie 3’s limit, but DeepMind research engineer Hang Qi noted that reaching that limit doesn’t guarantee that a scene will keep its consistency the whole time, according to Bloomberg . Google says it’s still working to improve complex physical interactions. One of its demos even includes a physics slip: A marble bust that drops onto a watermelon settles on its plinth when it should topple over the side. “There’s only so much that you can do with two minutes,” Google DeepMind product manager Diego Rivas said, per TechCrunch . “We’re still in the research journey. We’re not necessarily in the end product journey.” Behind the news: Genie 4 has plenty of company: The world models field is getting more crowded, although not every world model operates the same way. Like GWM Worlds 2 , the model Runway released in September, Genie 4 generates video in real time. Marble , from AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s startup World Labs, and HY-World 2.0 , an open-weights model from Chinese tech giant Tencent, build persistent 3D scenes instead. Robotics isn’t the only field disrupted by the new wave of world models. When Genie 3 opened to paying subscribers in January, it sparked a sharp selloff of video game stocks. In October, electric-vehicle maker Rivian bought world-model startup Third Dimension to bring self-driving simulation in house. The field is also consolidating. AMD agreed in September to buy World Labs for about $8.2 billion, and, per The Wall Street Journal , Amazon has been in talks to acquire Decart, whose products include world models for robotics and driving simulation. Genie 3 served as an environment for SIMA, DeepMind’s agent for 3D virtual worlds. Waymo later built a driving simulator on Genie 3 to generate unusual scenarios (things like a tornado or an elephant in the road). Runway has also pushed its world models toward robotics. In February it announced that robot-control policies acting inside a robotics version of its video model earned simulated scores that closely tracked their real-world results in tabletop tests. In September, Runway debuted a research preview of GWM Worlds 2 , a real-time world model with audio. It also announced Praxis-1 , a model for controlling real robots that it plans to release with open weights. Why it matters: Google’s clearest evidence that simulation can improve real robots comes from a different approach from other companies. A few weeks before Genie 4’s debut, Google showed Gemini 4 Argon writing physics simulations in the MuJoCo engine based on photos and video. From a single photo of a tabletop, Argon generated more than 4,500 practice episodes, and fine-tuning a robot-control model on them raised its real-world success rate from 56 percent to 75 percent. Google’s proposed path forward, which it calls hybrid world models, would combine elements of both the structured reasoning of language and code models with a generative model that renders pixels. Theoretically that could give generated environments reliable cause and effect, which is something video models often lack. We’re thinking: A good robot simulator lets plans fail, since robots learn from mistakes as well as successes. Genie 4 pairs its renderer up with a Gemini director that checks whether each step of a plan succeeded. This can accidentally drift the world toward whatever the intended outcome is. In the marble bust clip, the model itself seems to choose a neat landing on the plinth instead of the toppling over the side like physics says it should. Our question for DeepMind: Can a plan fail in Genie 4? We’d like to see that Apptronik robot hand mess up and drop a few checkers, too.
